meta.title: Wall Street Called This Fund 'Un-American' in 1976
meta.hook: In 1976, Wall Street mocked this fund as 'un-American.' It now anchors trillions of dollars.
meta.description: John Bogle launched the First Index Investment Trust at Vanguard on August 31, 1976, aiming to simply track the market instead of beat it. It raised just over $11 million against a $50-150 million goal and was ridiculed by critics — but the low-cost index approach it pioneered now underpins trillions of dollars in assets. Educational content only, not financial advice.

scenes.narration: John Bogle launched the First Index Investment Trust at Vanguard in August nineteen seventy-six.

visual.visual_intent: A man in 1970s business attire in an office setting, archival warm tone

scenes.narration: Instead of picking stocks, it simply held the entire market and tried to match it, not beat it.

scenes.narration: Bogle hoped to raise fifty to a hundred fifty million dollars. The fund raised just over eleven million.

visual.visual_intent: A small stack of cash beside a much larger empty outline space, symbolic of falling short, clean composition
visual.decision_reason: reported underwriting target vs actual raise, Fool.com/Kiplinger-sourced

scenes.narration: Critics called indexing a guaranteed path to mediocrity. Why settle for average?

visual.visual_intent: A financial newspaper section spread on a table, dim reading light
visual.decision_reason: represents contemporaneous critic sentiment, widely reported

scenes.narration: Within about two decades, that fund and the index-investing movement it sparked had grown into the hundreds of billions of dollars.

visual.decision_reason: qualitative growth framing to avoid implying an annual investment-return figure

scenes.narration: Bogle's bet was that low costs beat stock-picking skill over time. Index funds now hold trillions on that same bet.
